content.text: Scaling laws describe smooth, predictable gains: a model's loss falls as a power law as parameters, data and compute grow. Size is one lever, not the lever: a 70B model trained on more data beat models up to 530B. Many "abilities that appear suddenly" look sudden because the metric gives no partial credit. Choose a model by testing it on your task, not by its parameter count.

Your team adds invoice-field extraction. In the design review someone argues for the largest model in the family: "abilities only emerge at scale, small models just can't do this". It ships on the biggest tier. Months later a cost review runs a few hundred labeled invoices through the smallest model of the same family, and it extracts the fields just as well, at a fraction of the price and latency. Nobody had tested it, because a chart in a paper suggested small models score zero.
The common misconception
"Capabilities suddenly emerge past a magic parameter count, so the largest model is always the best choice." It has real evidence behind it:

items.text: Scaling works. Kaplan and colleagues found in 2020 that language-model loss falls as a power law with model size, data and compute, with some trends spanning more than seven orders of magnitude.
in 2022: few-shot tasks where performance stays near random for smaller models, then jumps well above random past a certain scale.
Within one model family, the larger model usually does score higher on public benchmarks.
Parameter counts make easy headlines, and "bigger is smarter" is a simple rule.

content.text: It's a half-truth. Scale matters a lot. But the gains are smooth in the quantity models are trained on, size is only one of three levers, and the threshold in those charts is not a universal number. The best model for you is the cheapest one that clears your bar.
What actually happens
Scaling laws are smooth curves
A
scaling law

relates a model's cross-entropy loss, how well it predicts the next token, to the resources spent on it. Kaplan and colleagues measured three: parameters, training tokens and training compute. Each gave a straight line on a log-log plot when the other two weren't the bottleneck, and details such as network width or depth mattered little within a wide range. There is no cliff in these curves: each tenfold increase buys a predictable, shrinking reduction in loss.
Size is one lever: Chinchilla

Kaplan's analysis suggested putting extra compute mostly into bigger models trained on relatively modest data. Hoffmann and colleagues at DeepMind revisited that in 2022 by training over 400 models, from 70 million to over 16 billion parameters, on 5 to 500 billion tokens. Their conclusion: for a fixed compute budget, model size and training tokens should grow equally, doubling one means doubling the other, and the large models of the time were undertrained.

They tested it with Chinchilla: 70B parameters, 1.4 trillion tokens, the same compute budget as their 280B Gopher. Chinchilla outperformed Gopher, GPT-3 (175B), Jurassic-1 (178B) and Megatron-Turing NLG (530B) on a large range of tasks, reaching 67.5% average accuracy on MMLU, a more than 7% improvement over Gopher. Being smaller, it also needs substantially less compute to fine-tune and run.
Where the sudden jumps come from

Wei and colleagues' arithmetic example, from BIG-Bench: GPT-3 stayed near zero for several orders of magnitude of training compute, then jumped at 13B parameters; LaMDA, on the same benchmark, jumped at 68B. They also reported 14 BIG-Bench tasks where PaLM 62B was above random while LaMDA 137B and GPT-3 175B were not, and wrote that scale is not the singular factor. The threshold moves with the model family, data and training.

Schaeffer and colleagues at Stanford proposed in 2023 that many such jumps come from the metric. Exact match gives credit only when every token of the answer is right, so a steady per-token improvement looks flat and then shoots up. This toy model family improves smoothly; watch what exact match does with it:

blocks.code:
import numpy as np

# Hypothetical model family whose per-token accuracy improves smoothly
sizes = np.logspace(8, 11, 7)                 # 100M to 100B parameters
per_token = 1 - 0.5 * (sizes / 1e8) ** -0.5   # a smooth curve, no jumps
LENGTH = 20                                   # tokens in each answer

for n, p in zip(sizes, per_token):
    exact = p ** LENGTH            # all 20 tokens must be right
    wrong = LENGTH * (1 - p)       # expected wrong tokens per answer
    print(f"{n:7.0e} params  per-token {p:.2f}  "
          f"exact match {exact:6.1%}  wrong tokens {wrong:4.1f}")

content.text: Exact match reads 0.0% and 0.1% for the two smallest models, then 3.2%, 15.5%, 35.8% and on up to 72.7%: a textbook "emergent ability". The expected number of wrong tokens per answer falls steadily from 10.0 to 0.3 over the same models. Nothing sudden happened to the models; the metric did it.

Schaeffer and colleagues tested this on real models. On InstructGPT/GPT-3 arithmetic tasks, switching from exact accuracy to token edit distance, on the same outputs, turned the jumps into smooth curves, and a larger test set showed small models above chance where they had looked like zero. In BIG-Bench, over 92% of the claimed emergent abilities appeared under one of just two metrics, multiple-choice grade and exact string match.

The debate isn't fully settled. Wei and colleagues noted that partial credit is "at best an incomplete explanation", since some classification tasks still show jumps, and Schaeffer and colleagues stress they don't claim models can't show emergent abilities. And all-or-nothing is sometimes what you need: an extraction is only useful if every field is right. But then the cliff comes from your answer length and strictness, it's predictable from partial-credit scores, and it doesn't sit at a magic size.

rows.text: Abilities switch on at a magic parameter count
The same arithmetic jump came at 13B for GPT-3 and 68B for LaMDA
Chinchilla 70B, with 4 times the data, beat Gopher 280B on the same compute
A sudden jump on a chart means a new ability
All-or-nothing metrics turn smooth per-token gains into cliffs
A small model scoring zero can't do the task
More test data and partial credit showed small models above chance
The largest model is always the best choice
The best choice is the cheapest model that passes your own evaluation

blocks.title: Record partial credit next to pass or fail

content.text: When you compare models, store a continuous score as well, such as the share of fields correct or the edit distance. It shows how close a smaller model is, and which fields fail, where pass or fail shows only zero.
A threshold on a public benchmark says little about your task. The scale where a jump appeared depended on the model family, the data and the metric, none of which are yours.
How to apply it in your project

Anthropic's model-selection guide puts it plainly: a good evaluation set, built from tests specific to your use case, is "the most important step in the process". One approach it recommends starts with a fast, low-cost model and upgrades only where testing shows a gap.

items.title: Build an evaluation from real inputs

content.text: Collect a few hundred real inputs with known correct outputs, including the hard and ugly ones.

items.title: Test the whole family, smallest first

content.text: Run every candidate model on the same set. Size alone won't predict which one clears your bar.
Track per-field accuracy or edit distance alongside pass or fail, so you see near misses and how to fix them.

items.title: Pick the cheapest model that passes

content.text: Weigh accuracy against price and latency per request, and rerun the evaluation whenever models or prompts change.
Key takeaways

items.text: Scaling laws are smooth: loss falls predictably as parameters, data and compute grow.
Size is one lever; Chinchilla 70B beat models up to 530B by training on more data.
Many "emergent" jumps come from all-or-nothing metrics applied to smooth improvements.
The scale where a jump appears depends on the model family, data and metric, not a magic number.
Choose the cheapest model that passes an evaluation built from your own task.
